description: A fungal foliar disease reported on neem and commonly associated with Alternaria alternata. It can begin as localized spotting and progress to blighting of affected leaf tissue.
typical_symptoms: Dark brown to black spots, often on yellowing tissue; spots may enlarge or merge; affected areas can become necrotic and leaves may dry or shed prematurely.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem leaves are normally deep green and intact, without dark necrotic spots, expanding blighted areas, or abnormal yellowing.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use: discard the visibly affected leaf rather than cutting around the lesions. Use separate, fully healthy neem leaves only after the plant is under control and normal quality checks are satisfied.
treatment_instruction: Remove heavily infected leaves and fallen debris; improve spacing and airflow; avoid prolonged wet foliage. If disease persists, use only a locally registered treatment for neem and follow the label and pre-harvest interval.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Active fungal spotting/blight and necrotic tissue make the affected leaf unsuitable as medicinal raw material. Use separate healthy leaves after the disease is controlled.

description: A bacterial foliar condition of neem. Bacterial leaf spot and vein-blight symptoms have been reported in neem, with Pseudomonas and Xanthomonas species among reported causal bacteria.
typical_symptoms: Water-soaked or angular dark spots, yellowing around lesions, vein blight, and sometimes shot-hole symptoms where dead tissue falls out; severe lesions may merge and contribute to leaf drop.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem leaves should not show water-soaked angular lesions, shot holes formed from dead tissue, dark bacterial-looking spots, or blighted veins.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use: discard leaves showing water-soaked, necrotic, shot-hole, or blighted symptoms. Do not try to salvage the affected leaf by trimming the visible spot.
treatment_instruction: Remove affected leaves, dispose of infected debris, sanitize cutting tools, avoid overhead watering and handling plants while wet, and reduce leaf-to-leaf splash. Seek confirmation before using any bactericide.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Visible bacterial-type infection, necrosis or blighting is incompatible with medicinal raw-material quality. The affected leaf should not be used.

description: A pest-damage class rather than a plant disease. Defoliating insects or other leaf-feeding pests remove leaf tissue and can reduce foliage substantially.
typical_symptoms: Missing or eaten leaf tissue, ragged or geometric chewing marks, partial skeletonization, damaged margins, drying of remaining tissue, and partial or severe defoliation.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem leaves retain complete leaflets and margins without extensive chewing, skeletonization, or unexplained loss of foliage.
medicinal_use_instruction: Do not use heavily chewed or contaminated leaves for medicinal preparation. Prefer a separate intact, healthy leaf from the same plant after the pest problem is controlled.
treatment_instruction: Inspect both leaf surfaces and shoots for larvae or eggs; hand-remove pests where practical; prune severely damaged leaves; conserve natural enemies. If an insecticide is needed, use only one registered for the crop and observe the label and pre-harvest interval.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Feeding damage does not prove that all medicinal compounds are lost, but substantial chewing and possible pest contamination reduce material quality. Prefer intact healthy leaves.

description: A progressive shoot-and-branch decline syndrome reported in neem. Phomopsis azadirachtae has historically been associated with neem dieback in published reports.
typical_symptoms: Drying starts at terminal shoots and progresses downward; crown thinning and defoliation may occur; inflorescence blight and premature wilting of fruits can accompany severe cases.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem shoots remain green and actively growing, without progressive drying from the tip toward the base or widespread branch death.
medicinal_use_instruction: Do not use leaves from dying, wilted, or visibly affected shoots for medicinal preparation. Harvest only separate healthy growth after the cause of dieback has been addressed and the plant has recovered.
treatment_instruction: Prune dead or affected shoots back into healthy tissue using sanitized tools; remove infected debris; reduce plant stress and correct drainage problems. Because dieback can have several causes, obtain plant-pathology confirmation if it continues.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Leaves from actively dying or severely declining shoots should not be used as medicinal raw material because the underlying cause and tissue quality are uncertain.

description: A visible stress/condition class, not a single confirmed disease diagnosis. Irregular yellowing in neem may be associated with nutritional deficiency, water/root stress, pest pressure, or systemic disease and therefore requires further diagnosis.
typical_symptoms: Patchy or uneven chlorosis, yellowing of tips or margins, mottled green-and-yellow areas, reduced vigor, drooping, and in some cases premature leaf fall.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem foliage is generally evenly green and vigorous rather than patchily chlorotic, mottled, or prematurely yellowing.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended when yellowing is strong or unexplained. Do not use the discolored leaf as medicinal material; choose a separate healthy green leaf only after the underlying stress or disease has been identified.
treatment_instruction: Do not apply a disease-specific treatment from yellowing alone. Check watering, drainage, root health, nutrition, pest activity, and other disease signs; correct the confirmed cause and monitor new growth.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Irregular yellowing is a nonspecific stress symptom. The cause and medicinal-material quality cannot be determined reliably from appearance alone.

description: A broad foliar blight syndrome in neem. Multiple fungal causes have been reported in different studies, so this class should not be treated as a single pathogen-specific diagnosis unless the dataset provides confirmed etiology.
typical_symptoms: Expanding brown to dark necrotic areas, large blighted patches, drying and collapse of affected tissue, and possible premature defoliation in severe cases.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem leaves lack large expanding necrotic patches, widespread blighting, and rapid drying of substantial portions of the lamina.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use: discard blighted or necrotic leaves. Do not cut away the brown area and use the rest of the same affected leaf.
treatment_instruction: Remove severely affected leaves and fallen debris; improve airflow; avoid prolonged leaf wetness and overhead irrigation. If a fungicide is required, first confirm the causal disease and use only a locally registered product according to the label.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Blighted and necrotic tissue is visibly deteriorated and may be pathogen-associated. The affected leaf should not be used medicinally.

description: An insect-mining damage class rather than a fungal or bacterial disease. Leaf-miner larvae feed within leaf tissue and create visible mines. The exact leaf-miner species on neem should be confirmed for the local dataset.
typical_symptoms: Pale or whitish serpentine tunnels or blotch-like mines inside the leaf, small feeding punctures, localized drying, and in severe cases premature leaf drop.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem leaves do not contain winding translucent mines, internal blotches, or characteristic feeding trails within the leaf blade.
medicinal_use_instruction: Do not use heavily mined leaves for medicinal preparation. Prefer separate, intact healthy leaves; do not rely on cutting around visible mines because larvae and damaged tissue may extend within the leaf.
treatment_instruction: Remove heavily mined leaves where practical, inspect new flush regularly, reduce nearby alternate hosts/weeds, and protect natural parasitoids. Use a registered pest-control product only if damage is severe and follow the pre-harvest interval.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Mining damage can leave some intact tissue, but internal feeding injury and possible pest contamination reduce suitability. Prefer separate undamaged leaves.

description: A combined condition representing simultaneous leaf-miner injury and powdery mildew symptoms. It should be treated as a mixed condition, not as one causal disease.
typical_symptoms: Serpentine or blotch-like mines within the leaf together with white to gray powdery fungal patches on the surface; yellowing, drying, or premature leaf drop may occur when damage is extensive.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem leaves lack both internal mining trails and white/gray powdery fungal growth.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use: discard leaves showing both mining injury and powdery fungal growth. Use only separate, healthy leaves after both problems are controlled.
treatment_instruction: Manage the two problems separately: remove heavily mined/mildewed leaves, improve airflow, reduce prolonged leaf wetness, monitor for miners, and conserve beneficial insects. Use only locally registered controls appropriate to each problem.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: This combines insect injury with active fungal growth, making the affected leaf unsuitable for medicinal raw material.

description: A rust-like foliar condition corresponding to the dataset label. A neem-specific causal rust fungus was not reliably verified in the sources reviewed, so this row intentionally describes the visible rust syndrome rather than naming a pathogen.
typical_symptoms: Powdery yellow, orange, rust-brown, or dark pustule-like spots on leaves, often accompanied by chlorosis and drying when infection is severe.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem leaves do not show rust-colored powdery pustules or spore-like masses on the leaf surface.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use: discard leaves showing rust-like pustules or substantial yellowing. Do not use the unaffected-looking portion of the same diseased leaf.
treatment_instruction: Remove and dispose of infected leaves and fallen debris, avoid overhead watering, improve airflow, and prune heavily affected shoots when appropriate. Confirm true rust before applying any fungicide.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Rust-like pustules and associated deterioration indicate active foliar disease. The affected leaf should not be used medicinally.

description: A visible yellowing/stress class rather than a single pathogen-specific disease. In a recent medicinal-leaf disease dataset, neem yellowing was described as generalized yellowing and drooping associated with nutritional stress or possible early systemic infection.
typical_symptoms: Generalized loss of green color, pale or yellow leaflets, possible drooping, and reduced visual vigor without necessarily having a distinct lesion pattern.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem leaves are normally deep green and firm rather than broadly yellow, pale, or drooping.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended when the leaf is broadly yellow or stressed. Use a separate healthy green leaf only after the cause has been corrected; yellowing alone does not identify a pathogen.
treatment_instruction: Check irrigation, drainage, root condition, nutrition, pests, and other disease symptoms. Correct the identified stress and monitor whether new leaves return to normal green growth.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: General yellowing is a nonspecific stress sign and does not reveal its cause or the concentration of medicinal constituents. Expert or agronomic verification is appropriate.

description: A fungal disease of neem reported as powdery mildew and associated with Oidium azadirachtae in forestry pathology references.
typical_symptoms: White powdery patches on the leaf surface that can enlarge and merge; severe infection may give the lamina a gray-white appearance and contribute to premature defoliation.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem leaves are clean and green without white or gray powdery fungal growth on the surface.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use: discard leaves with visible white/gray powdery growth. Do not wash or trim the affected area and then use the same leaf as medicinal material.
treatment_instruction: Remove heavily infected leaves, improve spacing and airflow, avoid conditions that keep foliage persistently humid, and clean up fallen material. If needed, use only a locally registered mildew treatment and follow the label and pre-harvest interval.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Visible fungal growth is incompatible with medicinal raw-material quality. Do not use the affected leaf.

description: A fungal web-blight disease reported on neem and associated with Rhizoctonia solani. Adjacent infected leaves can become connected by fungal growth.
typical_symptoms: Grayish-brown blotches that enlarge, silky or web-like fungal growth between nearby leaves, leaf curling, necrosis, and possible premature detachment.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem leaves lack gray-brown spreading blotches, necrotic webbed tissue, and fungal strands joining neighboring leaves.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use: discard leaves with webbing, spreading necrosis, or tissue collapse. Use separate healthy leaves only after the infection is controlled.
treatment_instruction: Remove blighted leaves and fallen debris, thin dense growth to improve airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation or prolonged wet foliage. If severe, confirm the diagnosis and use only a locally registered treatment.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Fungal webbing, necrosis and tissue deterioration make the affected leaf unsuitable for medicinal use.

description: A general neem leaf-spot class. Recent medicinal-leaf classification work describes this class by distinct brown spots with a circular ring. Several fungal leaf-spot pathogens are reported on neem, so the label should not imply one pathogen unless confirmed.
typical_symptoms: Clearly defined brown spots, often circular or ringed; lesions may increase in number or size, and some leaf-spot diseases can produce pale or gray areas and premature shedding when severe.
healthy_difference: Healthy neem leaves should be uniformly green without clearly defined circular brown lesions or expanding necrotic spots.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use when spots are active, numerous, or necrotic. Discard the affected leaf rather than cutting around the lesions; use a separate healthy leaf after the problem is controlled.
treatment_instruction: Remove severely spotted leaves and fallen debris, improve airflow, and avoid prolonged leaf wetness. Confirm the causal leaf-spot disease before applying any disease-specific treatment.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: A generic 'Spot' label may represent several causes. Because the exact condition is uncertain, medicinal suitability should be verified rather than inferred from the image alone.

description: A destructive betel-leaf rot syndrome commonly associated with Phytophthora species in betel pathology literature, especially under warm, wet and highly humid conditions.
typical_symptoms: Circular or irregular dark-brown water-soaked lesions that enlarge, become black or rotten-looking, and may spread rapidly during persistent humidity; severe infection can cause defoliation.
healthy_difference: Healthy betel leaves are glossy, green, firm and intact without water-soaked expanding brown-black rot lesions.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal or culinary use: discard any betel leaf showing water-soaked, soft, rotten, blackened, or expanding lesions. Do not cut away the rotten area and use the remainder.
treatment_instruction: Remove infected leaves/vines and plant debris, improve drainage, avoid waterlogging and frequent overhead irrigation, and keep foliage as dry as practical. For persistent Phytophthora problems, use locally recommended integrated management and only registered treatments.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Rotten, water-soaked or decomposing betel tissue should not be used for medicinal or culinary preparation.

description: A foliar spotting condition of betel. Colletotrichum-associated anthracnose/leaf spot is among the commonly reported causes, although the exact pathogen should be confirmed for a given dataset.
typical_symptoms: Small circular or oval brown to dark lesions, often with a yellowish border or halo; spots can enlarge, develop concentric patterns, merge, and form larger necrotic areas.
healthy_difference: Healthy betel leaves are evenly green and glossy without expanding brown necrotic spots, yellow halos, or coalescing lesions.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use when lesions are visible or expanding. Discard the affected leaf; harvest separate healthy leaves after the disease is under control.
treatment_instruction: Remove heavily spotted leaves and infected debris, improve airflow, reduce prolonged leaf wetness and splash, and maintain clean planting material. Use only a registered treatment after confirming the causal leaf-spot disease.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Active necrotic leaf spotting is substandard medicinal raw material. Prefer separate healthy leaves after the problem is controlled.

description: A low-moisture or post-harvest quality condition, not a disease diagnosis. A published Centella asiatica image dataset includes a Dried class, and dried Centella leaves are also intentionally prepared for products such as teas, decoctions and infusions.
typical_symptoms: Loss of fresh turgor, shriveled or dry texture, increased brittleness, reduced pliability, and possible darkening or other color changes associated with moisture loss.
healthy_difference: Fresh healthy Centella leaves are generally green, pliable and turgid rather than brittle, shriveled or markedly dehydrated.
medicinal_use_instruction: Conditionally suitable only if the leaf was intentionally dried using a hygienic, controlled process and shows no mold, decay, abnormal odor, insect contamination, or re-wetting. If the leaf dried unintentionally on the plant or shows deterioration, do not use it as medicinal material.
treatment_instruction: This is not a disease. If drying occurred on the living plant, check soil moisture, drainage, heat/sun stress, root health, and irrigation. If it is post-harvest drying, control drying conditions and store the material dry and protected from moisture and contamination.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Intentional hygienic drying can preserve medicinal constituents, but suitability depends strongly on the drying method, storage conditions and absence of mould or contamination.

description: A caterpillar-feeding abnormality reported for Centella asiatica. The source study calls this 'Worm Creep Disease', but biologically it is better treated as insect/pest damage rather than a pathogen-caused disease.
typical_symptoms: Chewed or missing leaf tissue, progressive feeding on both young and older leaves, ragged leaf edges, partial defoliation, and in severe cases extensive loss of leaves with mainly stems or petioles remaining.
healthy_difference: Healthy Centella asiatica leaves are intact, green and spreading, without extensive chewing, missing tissue, ragged margins, or progressive defoliation.
medicinal_use_instruction: Do not use heavily caterpillar-damaged, contaminated, or partly decomposed leaves for medicinal preparation. Prefer separate intact healthy leaves after the pest problem has been controlled. Do not assume that cutting around visible feeding damage makes a heavily affected leaf suitable.
treatment_instruction: Inspect both leaf surfaces and nearby growth for caterpillars and eggs; hand-pick small populations where practical and remove severely damaged leaves. Encourage natural enemies. If control is necessary, use only a product registered for the crop and pest, such as an appropriate caterpillar-specific biological control where locally permitted, and follow all label and pre-harvest instructions.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Caterpillar feeding removes tissue and may introduce frass or contamination. Heavily damaged leaves are poor-quality medicinal material; intact healthy leaves are preferred.

description: A mite-feeding abnormality reported for Centella asiatica. Red/spider mites feed on leaf sap and damage chlorophyll-containing tissue; this is pest damage rather than a fungal or bacterial disease.
typical_symptoms: Fine pale-yellow spotting or stippling on the upper leaf surface, loss of normal green color, possible bronzing, wilting or drying, reduced vigor, premature leaf fall, and sometimes fine webbing when mite populations are high.
healthy_difference: Healthy Centella asiatica leaves are evenly green and turgid, without widespread stippling, bronzing, mite webbing, abnormal wilting, or premature drying.
medicinal_use_instruction: Do not use leaves with heavy mite injury, extensive discoloration, webbing, contamination, or tissue deterioration for medicinal preparation. Prefer separate healthy leaves after the infestation has been controlled.
treatment_instruction: Check the undersides of leaves for mites and fine webbing. Keep plants adequately watered because drought stress can worsen mite problems, and use a firm water spray where practical to dislodge mites. Protect predatory insects and mites and avoid unnecessary broad-spectrum insecticides. If a miticide or other control is required, use only one registered for the crop and observe the label and pre-harvest interval.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Mite feeding causes physiological stress and visible tissue damage. Some medicinal constituents may remain, but heavily affected leaves have reduced and uncertain quality.

description: A nutritional disorder rather than an infectious disease. In Centella asiatica leaf-abnormality research, phosphorus deficiency is associated with restricted growth and dark green to purple pigmentation.
typical_symptoms: Stunted or reduced shoot growth, unusually dark or dull green foliage, reddish-purple or violet pigmentation in some leaves, smaller leaves, and reduced overall plant development. Symptoms may be more evident on older plant parts.
healthy_difference: Healthy Centella asiatica plants show normal spreading growth and appropriately green leaves without abnormal purple pigmentation, strong growth suppression, or unusually small leaves.
medicinal_use_instruction: Treat pronounced phosphorus-deficiency symptoms as a quality warning rather than an infectious disease. Prefer normally developed healthy green leaves for medicinal preparation. The visual appearance alone cannot establish the chemical quality or active-compound content of a deficient leaf.
treatment_instruction: Confirm the suspected deficiency with soil, growing-medium, or nutrient-solution testing before adding phosphorus. Check pH and root health because phosphorus can be present but unavailable. If testing confirms low available phosphorus, correct it using a phosphorus source appropriate for the growing system and recommended locally; avoid excessive phosphorus application.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Phosphorus deficiency can alter growth and secondary-metabolite accumulation, but the direction and magnitude cannot be determined reliably from an image. Nutrient/soil verification is recommended.

description: A serious basil disease caused by the oomycete Peronospora belbahrii. Symptoms often begin as yellowing before characteristic sporulation becomes visible on the underside of the leaf.
typical_symptoms: Angular or vein-bounded yellow/chlorotic areas on the upper surface, gray to purplish fuzzy/downy growth on the underside, followed by brown or black necrotic tissue as disease progresses.
healthy_difference: Healthy holy basil leaves are evenly green without vein-bounded yellow patches or gray-purple downy growth on the lower surface.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use: discard leaves with yellow angular lesions or gray/purple downy growth. Do not wash or trim an infected leaf for medicinal use.
treatment_instruction: Remove infected leaves/plants, reduce canopy humidity, improve spacing and airflow, water at the base, and avoid prolonged leaf wetness. Use resistant varieties where available and follow locally approved disease-management guidance.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Active downy mildew and associated tissue damage make the affected leaf unsuitable for medicinal raw material.

description: A web-blight condition in holy basil characterized in recent medicinal-leaf classification work by thin fungal webbing with necrosis and tissue death. The exact causal organism should be confirmed when pathogen-level diagnosis is required.
typical_symptoms: Thin web-like fungal growth across affected tissue, spreading brown or necrotic areas, tissue collapse or death, and possible sticking together of nearby affected leaf surfaces.
healthy_difference: Healthy holy basil leaves lack fungal webbing, spreading necrotic patches, and dead collapsed tissue.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use: discard leaves with fungal webbing, spreading brown lesions, or dead tissue. Use only separate healthy leaves after the disease is controlled.
treatment_instruction: Remove infected foliage and fallen debris, thin dense growth, improve airflow, and avoid overhead irrigation or prolonged humid/wet foliage. Confirm the causal organism before using any fungicide.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Fungal webbing and necrotic tissue indicate active disease and make the affected leaf unsuitable for medicinal use.

description: A visible leaf-spot condition in holy basil. In a recent medicinal-leaf disease dataset, Yellow Spot was characterized by a light yellow ring around an initial lesion and was described as compatible with bacterial or fungal spotting, not a single confirmed pathogen.
typical_symptoms: Localized yellow spot or pale yellow halo/ring around an initial lesion, sometimes followed by darker central tissue or enlargement of the affected area.
healthy_difference: Healthy holy basil leaves are more uniformly green and lack localized yellow-ringed lesions or spot-associated discoloration.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended when yellow spotting is pronounced or unexplained. Discard the affected leaf and use separate healthy green leaves only after the cause is identified.
treatment_instruction: Treat this first as a symptom class: remove badly affected leaves, reduce splash and prolonged wetness, inspect for pests and other disease signs, and obtain diagnosis if the condition spreads before choosing a pathogen-specific treatment.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Yellow spotting may arise from infectious or physiological causes. The image alone does not establish the cause or medicinal-material quality.

description: A pigmentation/physiological class rather than an infectious disease. Holy basil (Ocimum tenuiflorum / O. sanctum) occurs in green and purple subtypes. Research shows that purple Tulsi accumulates substantially more anthocyanin pigments in the foliage, with higher expression of anthocyanin-biosynthesis genes. Therefore purple or reddish-violet coloration can be normal varietal pigmentation rather than disease.
typical_symptoms: Purple, reddish-purple or violet coloration over part or much of the leaf, sometimes also visible on stems and inflorescences. When it is normal anthocyanin pigmentation, the tissue remains intact and does not show the necrotic lesions, fuzzy growth, water-soaking or rotting expected from disease.
healthy_difference: Green/Rama Tulsi is predominantly green, while purple/Krishna (Shyama) Tulsi naturally contains much more anthocyanin and may appear purple or reddish-violet. Thus pigmentation must be interpreted with the plant subtype and the absence or presence of true disease symptoms.
medicinal_use_instruction: Do not reject a holy basil leaf solely because of normal anthocyanin pigmentation. If the coloration is consistent with a healthy purple Tulsi subtype and there are no signs of disease, decay, pest contamination or other deterioration, the pigmentation itself is not evidence of poor medicinal quality. Visual assessment still cannot confirm chemical composition, contamination or clinical safety.
treatment_instruction: No disease treatment is required for normal varietal anthocyanin pigmentation. First confirm whether the plant is a naturally purple Tulsi subtype. If a normally green plant develops unexpected purple coloration together with poor growth or other stress symptoms, investigate environmental and nutritional stress rather than automatically treating it as an infection.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Normal anthocyanin pigmentation can be a healthy characteristic of purple/Krishna Tulsi and is not itself evidence of disease or reduced medicinal quality.

description: A fungal web-blight condition reported for Kalanchoe pinnata in medicinal-leaf classification work, characterized by mycelial webbing and confluent necrotic damage.
typical_symptoms: Gray mycelial or web-like growth, brown to dark necrotic spots that merge into larger affected areas, tissue death, and possible collapse of badly affected portions of the succulent leaf.
healthy_difference: Healthy Kalanchoe pinnata leaves are evenly green and succulent with intact edges and no gray webbing, spreading necrosis or abnormal discoloration.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use: discard leaves showing webbing, spreading necrosis, or soft/collapsing tissue. Do not salvage the same affected leaf by trimming.
treatment_instruction: Remove affected leaves and debris, improve airflow, avoid overhead irrigation and persistent humidity, and keep the succulent foliage dry. Confirm the causal disease before applying any treatment.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Active fungal web blight with necrotic tissue makes the affected leaf unsuitable for medicinal raw material.

description: A yellowing/stress condition rather than a single pathogen-specific disease. In a recent Kalanchoe pinnata dataset, the Yellow class was described as broad leaf yellowing while veins may remain greener, consistent with nutrient stress or possible early viral/systemic stress.
typical_symptoms: Generalized yellowing of much of the leaf blade, sometimes with greener veins, reduced normal green coloration, and no requirement for a distinct necrotic lesion.
healthy_difference: Healthy Kalanchoe pinnata leaves are evenly green, succulent and intact rather than broadly yellowed or chlorotic.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended when the leaf is broadly yellow, stressed, or deteriorating. Use separate healthy green succulent leaves only after the underlying cause is corrected.
treatment_instruction: Do not treat yellowing as a specific disease. Check overwatering, drainage, root health, light/heat stress, nutrition, and pests; correct the confirmed cause and monitor new growth.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Yellowing is nonspecific and may result from water, nutrient, root, environmental or disease stress. Suitability cannot be established from appearance alone.

description: A field-observed syndrome used as a classification label for Kalanchoe pinnata. It is characterized by extensive yellowing followed by marginal necrosis and tissue destruction; it should not be presented as a pathogen-specific disease unless independently confirmed.
typical_symptoms: Extensive chlorosis/yellowing, progressive browning or necrosis from leaf margins, damaged or dead edge tissue, and broader tissue destruction as the condition advances.
healthy_difference: Healthy leaves remain evenly green and succulent with intact living margins rather than widespread yellowing followed by marginal death.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended for medicinal use: discard leaves showing extensive yellowing together with marginal browning or necrosis. Do not cut off only the dead edge and use the remainder.
treatment_instruction: Remove badly affected leaves, improve drainage and airflow, avoid prolonged leaf wetness, and inspect roots and nearby foliage for additional symptoms. Because this label is a syndrome rather than a confirmed pathogen, diagnose the cause before treatment.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Extensive yellowing combined with necrotic/blighted tissue represents major deterioration. The affected leaf should not be used medicinally.

description: A broad pest-damage class for Kalanchoe pinnata (syn. Bryophyllum pinnatum), not a single disease. Published observations report leaf-feeding larvae such as the Red Pierrot (Talicada nyseus), whose larvae create blister-like mines that develop into blotches. Kalanchoe can also be attacked by sap-sucking pests such as aphids, scale insects, mealybugs and spider mites.
typical_symptoms: Blister-like or blotch-like mined areas, chewed or missing tissue, torn-looking portions of the leaf, yellowing or slight curling from sap feeding, sticky honeydew, white cottony mealybug masses, scale-like bumps, or fine webbing/stippling from mites. Symptoms vary with the pest.
healthy_difference: Healthy Kalanchoe pinnata leaves are thick, succulent and intact without feeding mines, chewing damage, abnormal yellowing/curling, honeydew, cottony pest masses or mite webbing.
medicinal_use_instruction: Do not use heavily insect-damaged, contaminated or deteriorating leaves for medicinal preparation. Prefer a separate intact healthy leaf after the infestation is controlled. Minor cosmetic injury alone does not prove that a leaf is unsafe, and an image cannot verify pesticide residues or chemical quality.
treatment_instruction: Inspect leaf surfaces, margins, axils and tender growth to identify the pest. Remove heavily affected leaves and hand-remove visible larvae or colonies where practical. Sap-sucking pests can often be reduced with a firm water rinse or an appropriately labelled insecticidal soap/horticultural treatment. Use only controls registered for the intended crop/use and follow all label directions.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Insect feeding can leave some intact medicinal tissue, but substantial damage and possible contamination reduce material quality. Prefer undamaged healthy leaves.

description: A composite visual-damage class rather than a single disease diagnosis. It can represent multiple simultaneous forms of foliar injury such as chewing, sap-feeding injury, discoloration, sooty deposits, deformation or necrosis.
typical_symptoms: A mixture of holes or pinholes, irregular or geometric chewing cuts, damaged margins, yellowing, distorted tissue, localized necrosis, and sometimes dark sooty coating associated with sap-feeding insects.
healthy_difference: Healthy curry leaves have intact, green leaflets without extensive chewing, holes, distortion, sooty coating, or multiple concurrent damage patterns.
medicinal_use_instruction: Not recommended when damage is extensive, mixed, contaminated, moldy, or necrotic. Prefer a separate intact healthy curry leaf rather than trying to trim and use a heavily damaged leaf.
treatment_instruction: Identify the components of the damage first: inspect for mites, psyllids, thrips, caterpillars, sooty mold, and disease lesions. Remove severely damaged leaves, manage the confirmed pest/disease separately, and use only products labeled for edible crops with the required pre-harvest interval.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Mixed foliar damage can involve chewing, sap-feeding, discoloration and contamination. Because the cause and retained quality vary, damaged material has low suitability.

description: A broad pest-damage class for curry leaf (Murraya koenigii), not a single disease. Curry leaf is attacked by both leaf-feeding insects and sap-sucking insects, including citrus butterfly larvae, psyllids, scales, mealybugs, aphids, tortoise beetles, leaf miners, whiteflies, leafhoppers and other defoliators.
typical_symptoms: Chewed or missing leaflet tissue, ragged or notched margins, partial defoliation, leaf mines, curling or distortion of tender growth, yellowing from sap feeding, sticky honeydew, and sometimes black sooty mould developing on honeydew. The exact pattern depends on the insect pest.
healthy_difference: Healthy curry leaves have intact green leaflets and normal tender growth without chewing holes, mining trails, abnormal curling, pest-associated yellowing, sticky honeydew or sooty deposits.
medicinal_use_instruction: For this visual-quality system, prefer intact healthy curry leaves. Do not use leaves with heavy feeding injury, extensive yellowing, frass, eggs, honeydew, sooty mould or other visible contamination. A lightly damaged leaf should not automatically be considered unsafe, but visual inspection alone cannot establish medicinal safety or pesticide-residue status.
treatment_instruction: Identify the pest type before treatment. Inspect tender shoots and both leaf surfaces; hand-pick large larvae where practical, remove severely infested leaves, use monitoring traps when appropriate, and conserve natural enemies. For citrus butterfly, extension guidance includes hand collection of larvae and Bacillus thuringiensis-based management. If a pesticide is necessary, use only a product registered for curry leaf/edible crops in the local jurisdiction and follow the label and pre-harvest interval.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Published evidence shows pest infestation can significantly alter chlorophyll, ascorbic acid, carotenoids and other metabolites in curry leaves. Healthy uninfested leaves are preferred.

description: A generic fungal-disease class for curry leaf (Murraya koenigii). The label should not be interpreted as one specific fungus unless the source dataset confirms it. A well-documented fungal leaf disease of curry leaf is anthracnose/leaf spot caused by Colletotrichum gloeosporioides; powdery mildew has also been reported on curry leaf. For a generic visual class, the safest wording is therefore 'fungal infection' rather than assigning a pathogen from the image alone.
typical_symptoms: Depending on the fungus, symptoms may include small dark or black necrotic spots, circular lesions that enlarge and become brown, tan or black, yellow halos around lesions, coalescing blackish patches, tip blight or burning, premature leaf drop, or white powdery fungal growth in powdery-mildew cases. Colletotrichum leaf spot on curry leaf is specifically reported to begin as small circular dark spots that enlarge and may develop visible black fungal fruiting bodies.
healthy_difference: Healthy curry leaf leaflets are intact, evenly green and free from necrotic spots, expanding brown/black lesions, yellow lesion halos, fungal fruiting bodies, powdery surface growth, tip blight and premature drying.
medicinal_use_instruction: Do not use curry leaves with visible active fungal infection, mould-like growth, substantial necrotic spotting or blight for medicinal preparation. Do not simply cut around a fungal lesion and use the remainder of the same affected leaflet. Prefer separate, fully healthy leaves after the disease has been controlled. Visual assessment cannot verify fungal toxins, microbial contamination, pesticide residues or the chemical potency of the material.
treatment_instruction: Remove heavily infected leaves and fallen diseased debris and keep them away from healthy plant material. Improve airflow and reduce prolonged leaf wetness and overhead splash where practical. Sanitize pruning tools. Because this is a generic fungal label, confirm the disease before selecting a fungicide. If chemical control is needed, use only a fungicide registered locally for curry leaf/edible crops and the confirmed disease, and strictly follow the product label and pre-harvest interval.
medicinal_suitability_assessment: Visible active fungal infection, mould-like growth, necrotic spotting or blight makes the affected curry leaf unsuitable as medicinal raw material.
